items_missed: No agenda statement — opened with 'seeing if I can get some more details from you before we send over a solid estimate' but never gave the 10-15 minute timeframe and never asked 'sound good?' for confirmation
Never asked about packing services at all, on a 4.5-hour out-of-town move where packing is a natural upsell and a real time variable
Never asked about storage stops or additional stops
No 'pricing is super simple' opener — he opened pricing with 'at the most granular level,' which frames it as complicated rather than simple

No Worries Damage Coverage never named — he only said 'the insurance that we place on your move,' with no $2,000 figure and no repair/replace/reimburse language, on a long-haul move carrying a TV, two mirrors and family items
No 'no hidden fees' pitch — no credit card fees, no fuel surcharge, no assembly fees never stated
Clock never explained as starting on-site when the contract opens; the 2.5-hour minimum and 15-minute proration only came out reactively after Brandon asked when payment is collected
Entire Save Your Ass prep speech missing — no 'prep before move day means a shorter move and a lower bill,' no consolidation examples, no 'take a carload' tip

No real booking attempt — said 'we do have the availability for you' and then handed the next step back to the customer with 'just shoot us an email give us a call' instead of asking to lock the date in
Never told Brandon to check the bolded details at the top of the email or to reply with corrections
Never asked 'any other questions before I let you go?' and never gave hours or how to reach the team
No Ecobox referral even though Brandon confirmed he'd be at the high end of 25 boxes
Missed the customer's opening cue — Brandon answered 'Hi, this is Tim' and Erik called him Brandon for the rest of the call without ever clarifying who he was speaking to
top_strength: The estimate build was genuinely excellent and is the model for how to narrate a long-haul quote. Erik ran a room-by-room inventory pass, then showed his math out loud: 2 to 2.5 hours to load because 'the load up portion is usually about twice as long as the unload,' 4 to 4.5 hours of drive because 'we're in big slow trucks and we don't go as fast as everybody else,' and an hour to an hour and a half to unload, landing at an eight-to-nine-hour day. He also proactively killed the customer's real objection — Brandon had read online that these moves take two days, and Erik walked him through why a one-day move works and that the crew absorbs the overnight themselves. He was equally clean on the travel charges, naming the $240 overnight and $1,680 return fee and then explicitly saying those two are 'the only two things that exist outside of the hourly rate.'
coaching_note: Erik, the highest-leverage fix is the Save Your Ass speech — it is worth ten points and you spent zero seconds on it, on the exact call type where it pays the most. This is an hourly job at $194/hr with a 4.5-hour drive baked in, so every box Brandon consolidates before you arrive is money off his own bill. After the inventory, say: 'Brandon, here's how you save yourself money — anything you can get boxed up and stacked by the door before we show up cuts the clock. Loose stuff in drawers, the kids' toys, photos off the walls, garden tools. And anything small enough to fit in your car, take a carload yourself. Does that make sense?' Second priority is the differentiators: you covered what's included beautifully but never named No Worries Damage Coverage, Meet Your Mover, or the On-Time Guarantee, and 'the insurance that we place on your move' does not land the way 'up to $2,000 to repair, replace, or reimburse accidental damages' does — especially with two mirrors and a TV going four hours down the road. Third, you built a good quote and then gave the close away: you told him availability exists and no deposit is required, then said 'just shoot us an email give us a call.' Ask for it instead — 'I've got Monday open, no deposit to hold it, want me to lock that in for you right now?' Last thing, and it's small but fix it: he said 'this is Tim' when he picked up and you called him Brandon for eleven minutes. Stop and confirm who you're talking to.
phone_presence_notes: Consistently warm and natural — 'I'm doing well, thank you for asking,' 'Absolutely!', 'my man' used easily, light self-deprecating humor about big slow trucks, and the customer closed with 'appreciate you,' though the unacknowledged 'this is Tim' and a lot of filler 'perfect/alrighty' kept it from a 5.
